title: The leper's offering
hookLine: on his alms round Kassapa stands by a man with leprosy, accepts a lump of rice from his hand, and eats it (Theragatha, Mahakassapa's verses)

cards: Morning, and an old monk walks into town with his bowl. This is the alms round: you don't choose the food, and you don't choose the giver. You stand, and you receive what's offered.
Today the one who wants to give is a man with leprosy, sitting and eating his own meal. Kassapa doesn't cross the street.
He goes and stands beside him, and the man lifts a lump of rice in his damaged hand and puts it in the bowl. These lines are Kassapa's own, in the verses the tradition gives him.

teach.h: A GIFT FROM A DAMAGED HAND.
teach.b: First, the offering. In the verses, the man's hand is so damaged by his illness that, as he places the food in the bowl, a finger falls in with it. The poem doesn't look away from that.

teach.h: HE ATE, AND FELT NO DISGUST.
teach.b: Kassapa says he sat down by a wall and ate that rice, and he adds the line that gives the story its force: while eating, and afterward, he felt no disgust. Third, why he tells it. These aren't boasting verses.
They sit among lines about a simple life: food from the alms round, medicine from what others discard, a seat at the foot of a tree.
For Kassapa, a gift is a gift, and the giver isn't graded first. The man with leprosy got to do what the other householders did: give, and be received. Fourth, what it isn't.
The story isn't asking anyone to ignore illness or take risks with health.
It's about what comes after a gift is taken: the quiet recoil, the polite thanks, the thing set aside later.
The verses say none of that came.

And this closes a week of great disciples: Ananda's tears and his night as arahant, the recital, Pippali and Bhadda leaving together, the worn robe, the strict practices, and now a lump of rice from an unexpected hand.

how: On the alms round in Theravada countries, monks walk in silence and receive whatever food is placed in the bowl, from any householder; Kassapa's verses about the leper's rice are one of the texts that show this way of receiving.

o: a fee paid to a teacher for lessons
a debt you must repay with interest

p: a lump of rice from his hand
sat by a wall and ate it

s: Kassapa took the rice and quietly threw it away
he sat down by a wall and ate it.
the story comes from Kassapa's own verses
the Theragatha, the verses of the elder monks, gives the lines to him.
the story asks people to ignore illness
it's about receiving a gift fully, without recoiling, while eating or after.

games.q: you're on your alms round. a man with leprosy wants to give you rice from his own hand. what do you do?
o: walk on to the next house.
stand beside him and receive it.
accept it, then leave it uneaten.
games.why: Kassapa stands by him, receives the rice, sits down by a wall and eats it, feeling no disgust.

practice: Think of a gift you accepted politely and quietly set aside: a clumsy present still in its box, advice you nodded at, a dish you praised and didn't finish.
Ask what was actually offered, and what it would take to use it, the way Kassapa ate the rice. Let yourself receive it fully now, and if thanks come up, let them come.

wordCard.voice: Dana, giving. What the man with leprosy offers Kassapa on his alms round, rice from a damaged hand, received and eaten without disgust. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali dana, giving: the man's offering is dana, received like any other.

carryVoice: Your line: he ate it. He didn't only accept the gift; he received it all the way. That's day seven hundred forty-two.
